newsitem.title: USA: Calif. submits initial plan under welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: Calif. submits initial plan under welfare reform.

text.p: California officials said Wednesday the state submitted its initial plan under the new federal welfare reform law, a move expected to provide nearly $200 million for the state in this fiscal year.
The state Department of Social Services formally unveiled the initial Temporary Assistance for Needy Families plan.

At a briefing, department officials said the state plan was sent to the federal government as a requirement of the new federal welfare reform law. Early submission of the state plan should result in a net benefit of about $195 million in the current fiscal year, the officials estimated.
The plan maintains existing state law and contains no new policy decisions or program provisions.

"I want to emphasize that the submission of this initial state plan today is not our new welfare redesign plan," Eloise Anderson, director of the Department of Social Services, told reporters. "This step should be viewed solely as an administrative action to generate maximum revenue for California this fiscal year to the tune of about $195 million and to put a large portion of that savings into helping to successfully transition...recipients from welfare to work."
The California plan only includes the minimum items needed to draw down the new federal funding, according to the department.

Submission of the state plan will result in the implementation of measures enacted previously by the state Legislature, including the 4.9 percent grant cut and the regional grant reductions, which had been delayed pending federal approval, the officials said.
California is one of 25 states that have submitted early state plans to begin receiving federal dollars.
The new federal welfare reform law requires a 45-day public review on the initial state plan.
The state's Department of Social Services said it would consult with local government and private sector organizations to obtain comments on the plan.

The new federal welfare reform law eliminates the open-ended federal entitlement program of Aid to Families with Dependent Children and creates a block grant for states to provide time-limited cash assistance for needy families.
That block grant replacing Aid to Families with Dependent Children, called the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, is to be implemented by states no later than July 1, 1997.
Under the federal law, however, states may implement earlier through the submission of a state plan.
